name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of using AI systems that answer legal questions by first fetching relevant primary and secondary sources, then generating a response tied to those sources. It covers case law search, statutory and regulatory research, and drafting support where citations must be traceable. The aim is to reduce fabricated citations and to keep the lawyer in control of the analysis. It sits within legal research and case strategy, not as a replacement for professional judgment.

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of using AI systems that answer legal questions by first fetching relevant primary and secondary sources, then generating a response tied to those sources. It covers case law search, statutory and regulatory research, and drafting support where citations must be traceable. The aim is to reduce fabricated citations and to keep the lawyer in control of the analysis. It sits within legal research and case strategy, not as a replacement for professional judgment.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on a combination of a document store or search index holding legal texts, an embedding model that turns passages into vectors, and a retrieval layer that finds candidate passages for a query. Many implementations use a vector database alongside a traditional keyword index, often called hybrid search. The generation model then reads the retrieved passages and produces an answer with citations. Some tools connect directly to commercial legal databases through APIs, while others index a firm's own document collection.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins by breaking source documents into chunks, embedding them, and storing them for fast similarity search. A user query is embedded and matched against the index, then a reranking step selects the most relevant passages. The language model is prompted to answer only from those passages and to cite them, and a verification step checks that each citation exists and supports the claim. Practitioners review the output, check the cited authorities, and refine the query or the source set as needed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk questions include copyright and licensing of the underlying legal texts, confidentiality of client documents fed into the system, and privilege concerns when third-party models are used. Provenance matters because an answer is only as good as the retrieved source, and a citation that looks correct may still be misread or outdated. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows how active these disputes are. Firms also need to manage accuracy, bias in retrieval, and the risk of unauthorized practice of law if outputs are not reviewed by a licensed attorney.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward tighter integration with authoritative databases, better citation verification, and audit trails that record which sources were retrieved and how they were used. Regulation of AI in legal services is moving, with 219 compliance and regulation pages and 6978 state AI bills tracked on this site, so expectations for transparency and accountability are likely to grow. Retrieval methods are also improving, with graph-based retrieval and multi-step reasoning that can follow citations across cases. The likely outcome is that retrieval grounding becomes a standard expectation for any AI tool used in legal research, rather than a special feature.
